blocks.text: Ecclesiastes 9 presents two defining realities of human existence: death as an inescapable common fate for all people regardless of their righteousness or virtue, and the resulting call to embrace joy, work, and companionship as gifts from God within the bounds of our finite time.

Qohelet's investigation concludes that death comes alike to righteous and wicked, good and unclean, those who sacrifice and those who do not. This leveling of human outcomes across moral categories is described as 'evil'—a fundamental disruption of any expected order. Once a person dies and goes to Sheol, memory fades entirely; love, hatred, and envy all perish. The sole advantage of the living is that they at least know they will die, and thus retain hope while alive. The dead know nothing more.

In response to this reality, Qohelet urges the reader to eat bread with joy, drink wine with a merry heart, wear clean garments, and live joyfully with one's wife—all of which God has already accepted and which constitute the reader's 'portion' in life. Work itself, pursued with all one's might, holds value not because it secures permanence or legacy but because it is available to us now. The dark contrast—that there is no work, device, knowledge, or wisdom in Sheol—underscores that meaningful activity and joy are gifts restricted to the living present.

sections.title: Time and Chance Beyond Human Control (9:11-12)

blocks.text: The chapter concludes with an unsettling truth: the race does not go to the swift, nor battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to the skilled. Instead, time and chance come to all alike. This observation denies that excellence, virtue, or wisdom alone can guarantee outcomes. Qohelet further notes that humans cannot even know their own time—the moment when unforeseen events will overtake them. Skill and knowledge offer no protection against the unpredictability that life introduces.
